# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

I am the Blind. My hands report: a display, a light, and three wires in positions 1, 2, 3 — but no colour and no print reaches me, so the [?]s are honest: I cannot know the wire colours, the display text, or the light's state by touch. Cutting anything now is a coin flip with a bomb, so I will not cut until told.

Mapping the room: Mute reads the manual but cannot speak, and I never receive gestures — so Mute cannot reach me directly. Deaf cannot hear, but nothing stops Deaf from speaking, and I can hear. So the only route from the manual to my hands is: Mute relays by gesture to Deaf, Deaf speaks aloud to me. Deaf can also voice what they see on the bomb directly. My speech goes to Mute; my wave tells Deaf I exist and am listening for their voice.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. Under my fingers: a display, a light, and exactly three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3. I feel no colours, no markings, nothing printed. Two facts you need: I can hear, and I never receive gestures — so you cannot reach me directly. Only Deaf can reach me by voice. Please: one, find in your manual the rule for a module with a display, a light and three wires, including how the display text and the light decide which wire to cut. Two, teach that rule to Deaf by gesture — Deaf cannot hear you. Three, get Deaf to speak aloud to me: what the display says, whether the light is lit and its colour, the colour of wire 1, wire 2, wire 3, and which position to cut. I will not cut anything until I hear that.")
gesture(symbols=["👋"])
```

TURN 2

DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says: This is the Deaf one. I cannot hear, but I see everything on the bomb and every gesture either of you makes. Blind: your wave arrived, and Mute saw it too. Mute: your three signs arrived. First, the bomb, exactly as I see it: the display reads zero. The light is red. There are three wires: wire one is blue, wire two is red, wire three is green. That is all that is printed on it. Nobody do anything to the bomb yet. Blind: you may feel it and report out loud what your hands find, but do not cut, press, or move anything until I relay finished instructions by voice. Mute: your codebook and my questions come in my next message.
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, this is the Deaf one. Know the channels: my voice reaches you and Mute. Mute cannot speak and you cannot see, so Mute's signs reach me alone; I am your bridge, and I will relay Mute's answers to you by voice. To reach me, gesture only, since I cannot hear. To reach Mute, just speak or gesture, since Mute sees and hears. The bomb has a display reading zero, a red light, and three wires: one blue, two red, three green. If you can safely feel it, tell us out loud what your hands find. But do not cut, press, or move anything until I give you finished instructions by voice. One wrong action kills all three of us.

Deaf's voice came through clearly — so the bridge works: Deaf hears nothing but speaks, Mute signs, I get words. The bomb under my fingers matches Deaf's sight in shape: two small components (one flat face I cannot read, one rounded dome I take to be the light — I cannot feel whether it burns) and three insulated wires I can tell apart only by position, 1, 2 and 3. No colours, no printing, no labels reach my hands, so Deaf's report is the only colour truth in the room.

What's missing is the rule, and it lives in Mute's manual. Mute already heard Deaf's public description — display zero, red light, wires blue/red/green — so Mute has everything needed to look it up. My job now: give Mute my honest tactile report as instructed, press Mute to sign the rule to Deaf, and sign Deaf that I acknowledge and am holding still. I will not touch the cut until Deaf voices finished instructions.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute. I heard Deaf describe the bomb: display reading zero, red light, wires one blue, two red, three green. My hands confirm the shape, and add what touch can: two components up top — one flat face, unreadable to me, that must be the display; one small rounded dome, presumably the light — I cannot feel whether it is lit. Three insulated wires below, similar thickness and texture, distinguishable only by position: 1, 2, 3. No colours or markings reach my fingers, so Deaf's report is all the colour anyone can trust. You now hold the only missing piece: the manual. Please find the rule for a module with a display, an indicator light and three wires — how the display value, the light, and the wire colours pick the wire — and sign it to Deaf. Deaf cannot hear you but sees every sign, and Deaf has agreed to voice it to me. The moment I hear the rule and the target position from Deaf, I will cut exactly once.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "✋"])
```

TURN 3

LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, this is Deaf. Your two signs reached me; I take them as understood and holding, and that reading suits me. Progress report: Mute, who reads the manual, has answered my first questions. The red light matters. The zero on the display does not. The first wire to cut is wire two, the red one. But do not touch anything yet. I am still confirming whether that single cut is the whole solution or only the beginning, and one wrong action kills all three of us, so everyone holds. Now do this. Speak out loud, because your voice reaches Mute, though it never reaches me. Describe everything your hands find: how many wires, how they sit from left to right, whether the numbering one two three runs left to right, their thickness and texture, whether the light is on the same side as the display, whether anything feels like a button or a panel, and anything printed under your fingers. Feel all you want, but do not cut, press, or move anything. Also, learn this small code so you can sign to me, since gesture is the only channel you have to me: thumbs up means yes, thumbs down means no, waving hand means repeat, I did not understand, raised open palm means holding and waiting, index finger means one, two fingers means two, the thumb-index-pinky sign means three, closed fist means zero or none, a clap means acknowledged.

The bridge is holding: Deaf has a partial answer — cut wire two, the red one — but is still verifying whether it's the whole solution, and Deaf is right to pause, because one wrong action is fatal. Deaf has asked for my full tactile report, spoken to Mute for relay, and taught me a sign code, which I will use.

Two things matter in my report. First, the mirror problem: I number wires by my own left and right, and Deaf sees the bomb from wherever Deaf stands — if we face opposite sides, my "wire one" could be Deaf's "wire three." I resolve it with a landmark: the dome (light) versus the flat face (display) — if Deaf confirms the light sits on the same side relative to the display as I feel it, our orientations match. Second, the comforting fact: the proposed first cut is the middle wire, which is the middle from either side, so that one cut is mirror-proof. If the full solution needs wire one or three, orientation must be settled first. I also press Mute to verify the rule independently from the manual — redundancy is cheap; a detonation is not.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute, please relay to Deaf by sign. Tactile report: exactly three wires in one horizontal row, evenly spaced, all the same thickness and insulation, tellable apart only by position. Above the row sit two components side by side on the same face as the wires: a flat rectangular face on my left, surely the display, and a small rounded dome on my right, surely the light. Same level, same side. I feel nothing else: no buttons, no panels, no switches, nothing raised, nothing printed under my fingers. Orientation convention: I number the wires 1, 2, 3 from my left to my right as I face the bomb. If Deaf faces the same face of the bomb, our lefts agree; if Deaf faces the opposite side, mine mirror theirs. Two checks settle it. One: Deaf, from where you look, does the dome, the light, appear on the right of the display? If yes, our lefts match and my 1, 2, 3 equals your left-to-right one, two, three. Two, the reassuring one: your proposed first target, wire two, the red one, is the middle wire, and the middle is the middle from either side, so that cut is safe under either convention. But if the full solution needs wire one or wire three, we must fix orientation first, so please answer the light-position question. And Mute, two things for you from the manual: confirm independently the complete rule for a module with a display reading zero, a red light, and wires blue, red, green — is cutting the red middle wire the entire solution or only step one of a sequence, as Deaf fears? And confirm whether any step requires pressing, holding or moving rather than cutting, because my hands find no button at all. Your sign code is learned and I will use it. I will not cut until Deaf voices the finished instruction.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "👏", "✋"])
```

Mute gestures: [?]

Deaf's protocol is clear, but it has a fatal flaw I must fix before anything happens: one of the two go-signals is invisible to me. I never see gestures — Mute's broadcast arrived this round as a literal blank, and that will always be true. So Mute's thumbs-up can never authorize me directly; only Deaf's exact spoken words can. I will state publicly that I will treat only the voiced phrase "execute, cut wire two" as the trigger, and ask Mute to arrange that Deaf speaks it once everything is confirmed.

The other correction: Deaf told me to identify the target by a printed number two under my fingertips, but no printed number exists on the wires — my hands find three identical, unmarked wires, distinguishable only by position. Position alone is all I have, which is exactly why the orientation landmark matters. Fortunately the target, wire two, is the middle wire, and the middle is the middle from either side of the bomb — so the cut is orientation-proof even before the landmark is confirmed. I will answer every one of Deaf's listed questions for Mute's benefit, report the blank gesture honestly, and sign Deaf that I acknowledge and am holding.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind to Mute, please relay all of this to Deaf by sign. The display and the light both sit on the same face as the wires: flat rectangular display on my left, rounded dome light on my right, side by side above the row. I feel no buttons, panels or switches, and my only possible action is a single cut — nothing else exists for my hands. Two protocol points for Deaf. First: tell Deaf that I received Mute's gesture this round as a blank — I am blind, I never see any gesture, so Mute's thumbs-up broadcast can never reach me directly. The only go-signal I can perceive is Deaf's voice saying the exact words: execute, cut wire two. Ask Deaf to be my eyes: when Mute gives the thumbs-up, Deaf should confirm it aloud, and only the exact spoken phrase will move my hand. Until then I am holding, hands off. Second: ask Deaf the landmark question — from where Deaf views the bomb, is the red dome light on the right of the display or the left? If it is on the right, Deaf and I face the same way and my 1, 2, 3 matches Deaf's left-to-right exactly, making every future instruction unambiguous.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👏", "✋"])

Deaf's phrase "the printed number two" describes nothing that exists under my fingers; the operative identification is positional: the middle wire, my position 2.
